results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Resonating Lute, Inevitable Defeat and Jeskai Revelation.
results.text:
I built a four-color control deck (blue, red, white, black) that ramps with Resonating Lute. It uses the Jeskai Control shell from the menu, splashes black for Inevitable Defeat, and is labeled a brew. No published list plays all three of your cards together.

**The plan:** In the early turns, Lightning Helix, No More Lies, Get Lost and Fire Magic keep you alive while Consult the Star Charts and Stock Up dig for Lute. Once Lute is out, each land taps for two mana of any one color for instants and sorceries. That makes Jeskai Revelation (7 mana) castable off four lands on turn 5. It also lets you cast Inevitable Defeat (exile any nonland permanent, can't be countered, swings life 3 each way) in any colors using two lands. When your hand is at seven cards or more, Lute's tap ability draws you a card each turn.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Jeskai Control with a black splash (chosen).** It's the only shell where all three cards already show up: Jeskai Control runs Lute and Revelation, and the "Rogue" four-color lists pair Defeat with Revelation, Helix and No More Lies.
2. **The Lessons shell.** It plays Lute (1 list), but its cheap spells barely use Lute's doubled mana, and it has no natural spot for a three-color card like Defeat.
3. **A Lute "big spells" ramp deck with more spree and sweeper spells.** It's weaker because it gives up the proven early interaction you need against Prowess and Landfall, which are 37% of the field.

I chose the first because Lute's real job is to fix colors and double your mana, and that mostly helps a four-color deck full of instants like this one.

**How it fits together:**
- **Mana base:** 26 lands, like Jeskai Control: 18 blue, 14 red, 19 white and 11 black sources. Great Hall of the Biblioplex and Starting Town make any color, which covers Defeat's three colors before Lute arrives.
- **Mystical Teachings:** Works as a fourth Revelation or a fifth Defeat. Its flashback ({5}{B}) is easy to pay with Lute mana.
- **Fire Magic:** The deck checker flagged it as rarely played. I kept it because its top tier (3 damage to every creature) is a good use of Lute mana against go-wide boards. Burst Lightning only hits one target.

**Honest odds:**
- You'll naturally draw Lute by turn 4 in about 53% of games, before counting the card-draw spells that dig for it.
- The checker says you'll draw every card in my listed win sequence by turn 8 in under 1% of games. That's expected: the sequence is a sample, not a combo you have to assemble. In practice you win by stacking repeated Revelations, Defeats and Helixes, with Monk tokens and burn doing the last damage.

The 15-card sideboard covers Prowess and Landfall (Seam Rip, Pyroclasm, Flashfreeze), the Dimir decks (Duress, Negate, Disdainful Stroke), and graveyard decks (Rest in Peace).

--- After review ---
I made the reviewer's fix: both copies of Stock Up are out, and 2 Marang River Regent // Coil and Catch are in. The deck was accepted with no warnings and is still exactly 60 cards.

**Why the swap helps:**
- **It's an instant.** Coil and Catch costs {3}{U}, draws three and discards one. You can pay for it with Lute mana at the end of your opponent's turn. Stock Up is a sorcery, so it tapped you out on your own turn.
- **It fills your hand.** Coil and Catch gets you closer to 7 cards, which is when Lute's own draw ability turns on.
- **It's a finisher.** After you cast Coil and Catch, the card gets shuffled back into your library. Later you can cast the 6/7 flying Dragon, which returns up to two other nonland permanents to their owners' hands when it enters. Before this, the deck had nothing to close games with except burn and the Monk tokens from Revelation. One catch: the Dragon costs {4}{U}{U}, and Lute mana only pays for instants and sorceries, so you have to cast it off your normal lands.

I added the Regent to the win line as the card-draw and finishing step. Nothing else changed in the main deck or sideboard.

**On the odds:** the check tool says you'll have drawn every card in the win line by turn 8 in only 0.6% of games. That number is low because the line names six specific cards, and the tool doesn't count tutors or card draw. Consult the Star Charts, Coil and Catch and Mystical Teachings are there to find the pieces. You don't need every card in the line to win; Lute plus a steady flow of Defeats and Revelations is the real plan.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around The Jolly Balloon Man, Sewer-veillance Cam and Bloom Tender.
results.text:
I built a 4-color brew (green-white base with blue and red splashes) on top of the Aang deck's green ramp core: Llanowar Elves, Gene Pollinator, Spider Manifestation, Nature's Rhythm, Brightglass Gearhulk, Ouroboroid and one Craterhoof Behemoth. It's legal at 60 cards with a 15-card sideboard. Badgermole Cub is currently banned, so it isn't in the list.

**The plan:** Bloom Tender adds one mana for each color among your permanents. Spider Manifestation and Balloon Man count as red, Sewer-veillance Cam as blue, and Seam Rip and Gearhulk as white, so Tender usually makes 3–4 mana by itself.
- From turn 3, Balloon Man copies Bloom Tender. The copy has haste, so it taps for another 4 mana right away.
- You then cast Craterhoof, or cast Nature's Rhythm with X=8 to put it onto the battlefield.
- Balloon Man copies Craterhoof, which gives every creature +X/+X and trample a second time.
- Flash in Cam: when it enters it untaps Balloon Man, so you can copy Hoof a third time, or it untaps Tender for more mana.

**Which direction I picked:**
- **Chosen:** this Aang/Selesnya ramp shell plus red and blue.
- **Rejected:** an Azorius Blink version using Balloon Man to copy Floodpits Drowner and Aang. It had too little green to make Bloom Tender good.
- **Rejected:** a Formidable Speaker untap engine. I tested it for an infinite combo and found none, because each copy only gives back one untap.

The ramp shell won because it's the only one where all three cards do real work: Tender makes the mana, Balloon Man doubles Craterhoof, and Cam untaps one of them for an extra use.

**Odds and weak spots:**
- You draw a Balloon Man by turn 4 only about 53% of the time. You'll have at least one mana creature by then about 96% of the time.
- The checker says you naturally draw every card in the full combo by turn 5 in only about 1% of games. That number ignores tutors: Nature's Rhythm and Formidable Speaker find Craterhoof or Balloon Man, and Gearhulk fetches Cam.
- On a normal draw, expect a big Ouroboroid or Gearhulk attack, plus a Craterhoof kill on turn 5 or 6.
- The deck has 21 lands, below the Aang deck's 22.6, because it runs 15 mana creatures.

The sideboard is aimed at Prowess and Lessons, the two most common decks in the current results. It has Erode, Get Lost, Disdainful Stroke, Spider-Sense, Pawpatch Formation, Rest in Peace, Soul-Guide Lantern and Beza.

--- After review ---
I made both suggested fixes and resubmitted the deck. It's still 60 cards, legal, and wins with the same line.

1. **Quantum Riddler → second Craterhoof Behemoth.** The Riddler is a five-mana flyer that draws a card. It does nothing for the Tender → Balloon Man → Hoof line, and the four Sewer-veillance Cams already give Bloom Tender its blue. A second Hoof means you can draw the finisher on its own, so Balloon Man has something to copy when you don't have Nature's Rhythm. That makes six ways to get Hoof: 2 Hoof and 4 Rhythm.

2. **Meltstrider's Resolve → third Seam Rip.** The aura makes your creature fight, and it gives +0/+2 but no extra power. Most of your creatures are 1-power mana dorks, so the fight usually loses or costs you part of your mana engine. Seam Rip costs W and exiles an opponent's permanent with mana value 2 or less, so it doesn't risk a creature. It's also a white permanent, which adds a color for Bloom Tender.

**How often the full line comes together:** The check says you'll have drawn every card in the line by turn 5 in only about 2.3% of games. That number counts Craterhoof and Sewer-veillance Cam as separate cards you have to draw. It doesn't count Nature's Rhythm finding Hoof for you, so the real rate is higher. Still, the complete double-Hoof turn is a ceiling, not something to expect most games. Often the deck will win with one Hoof trigger plus the mana from Tender and Balloon Man.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Dáin's Company, Dwarven Mauler and Kíli the Resourceful.
results.text:
I built **Boros Dwarves Equipment**, a brew. No published list has ever played these three cards together, so this has never been tried in tournaments.

**The plan:** Dwarven Mauler comes down on turn 1. It makes equip costs {2} cheaper when they target it, so Leyline Axe (equip {3}) costs just {1} to put on it. That gives you a 3/2 with double strike and trample on turn 2 or 3. If the Axe is in your opening hand, it can start the game on the battlefield for free. On turn 2, Dáin's Company looks at your top four cards for another Dwarf or Equipment, and it has lifelink while you control another Dwarf. Kíli the Resourceful draws a card when another Dwarf or Equipment enters (once per turn). Once you control three artifacts and/or legendaries, Kíli makes your first equip each turn free. The many legendary Dwarves (Giott, Thorin, Dáin Ironfoot, Fíli) plus cheap Lavaspur Boots get you to three quickly.

**How it wins:** Giott and Dáin Ironfoot are the finishers. Dáin gives every equipped attacker double strike, and Giott already has it, so the equipment doubles up. The deck aims to win around turn 5. Burst Lightning, Chainsaw and Mjölnir clear blockers. The full line needs specific cards, so it only comes together in a small share of games (the checker put having every card in it by turn 5 at about 0.1%). The deck normally wins by attacking with whatever equipped Dwarf it has.

**Odds:** You see at least one of Mauler or Kíli by turn 3 about 70% of the time, and at least one of the 12 Equipment about 89% of the time. Dáin's Company's dig pushes both numbers up.

**Three directions I considered:**
1. **The one I built:** Boros legendary Dwarves with Equipment, using the menu's Boros Aggro package. That means its dual lands (Sacred Foundry, Inspiring Vantage, Sundown Pass) and its Burst Lightning.
2. **Big Equipment cheats:** Ultima Weapon or Genji Glove, made affordable by Mauler and Kíli.
3. **Burn-heavy Boros Aggro:** the menu's Hired Claw and Shock shell with the Dwarves added in.

I chose the first because every Dwarf and Equipment in it feeds all three requested cards at once: Company has more to find, Kíli draws more, and Mauler has more to equip. The other two would dilute that.

**Other choices:**
- **Three Kíli:** It's legendary, so a second copy in hand is often stuck there.
- **Two Chainsaw:** The checker noted that real decks rarely play it and choose Firebending Lesson or Impractical Joke instead. I kept it because it's an Equipment, so it also feeds Company, Kíli and Mauler, and those two spells don't.
- **22 lands:** The curve is low. The Boros Aggro lists I borrowed the mana from average about 23.

The 15-card sideboard is aimed at Prowess, Lessons and graveyard decks: Sear, Abrade, Lightning Helix, Shock, Magebane Lizard, Ghost Vacuum and Rest in Peace.

--- After review ---
I made the reviewer's fix. The revised deck is submitted and accepted.

**What changed**
- **Cut 2 Fíli the Pathfinder.** It costs 4 mana ({3}{W}), so it was competing for the turn-4 slot with Mjölnir and Dáin Ironfoot. The deck wants to win around turn 5 with cheap Dwarves carrying equipment, and Fíli didn't fit that.
- **Added a 4th Kíli the Resourceful.** It's one of the cards you asked to build around, and it only costs 2. It draws a card the first time each turn another Dwarf or Equipment enters. Once you control three or more artifacts or legendaries (Storied), your first equip each turn is free.
- **Added a 4th Thorin Oakenshield.** It's a 2-mana 3/2 legend with trample, and it also counts toward Storied. Once Storied is on, it gives all your artifacts and creatures ward {1}.

The deck now has 6 four-drops instead of 8, with 30 cards at 1–2 mana, an average mana value of 2.05, and 22 lands. The deck check reported no errors or warnings.

**One risk:** Kíli and Thorin are both legendary, so running 4 of each means you'll sometimes draw a second copy you can't use. I think that's worth it for consistency. Each one is cheap enough that the extra copy is still a playable 2-drop once the first dies.

**About the win line:** the submission tool said that in 0% of games you've drawn all 8 cards named in the win line by turn 5. That number expects every card in the sequence to be in hand, which won't happen. The line is just an example of how a game can go, and the tool doesn't simulate card draw or Dáin's Company's dig. In practice the deck wins with any cheap Dwarf carrying any of its 12 Equipment, and Burst Lightning finishes off the opponent.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Greedy Freebooter, The Sackville-Bagginses and Umbral Collar Zealot.
results.text:
I built **Orzhov Aristocrats**, a brew that was accepted at 60 cards with a 15-card sideboard. No published list in recent results plays your three cards together, so there was no existing shell to start from.

**Directions I considered:**
1. Orzhov aristocrats, using the Lifegain deck's mana base and its cheap white removal (Erode, Seam Rip).
2. Rakdos treasures (Crime Novelist, Reckless Lackey, Garna).
3. Mono-black rats (Voracious Vermin, Lord Skitter).

I picked Orzhov because white-black has the most cards that punish the opponent every time you sacrifice something: Popular Egotist, Vito and Teysa. It also gets the best cheap removal.

**The plan:** Greedy Freebooter and Nesting Bot come down early. When they die they leave tokens behind: Freebooter makes a Treasure, Nesting Bot makes a Servo. Umbral Collar Zealot can sacrifice them at any time.
- **The Sackville-Bagginses** turns your token sacrifices into damage: each one makes the opponent lose 1 life. That includes cracking a Treasure for mana.
- **Popular Egotist** adds another lost life, plus 1 life for you, on every sacrifice. With both out, each token is a 2-point hit.
- **Tolls of War, Bitterbloom Bearer and Teysa** keep making new tokens. Teysa works especially well: the life loss triggers her Clue every turn, and each Clue that dies makes a flying Spirit.
- **Vito** finishes the job, and the deck aims to win around turn 6.

**Mana:** 22 lands, borrowed from Lifegain, with 21 black sources and 19 white. The deck checker found no problems with it compared to real Lifegain lists.

**Honest odds:**
- You see Zealot by turn 4 in only about 53% of games. That's less of a problem than it sounds. Treasures can sacrifice themselves, Egotist is a second outlet, and Fountainport can sacrifice tokens too.
- At least one of Sackville, Egotist or Vito shows up by turn 4 about 83% of the time.
- Some token-maker shows up by turn 4 about 95% of the time.
- The 0.2% figure from the checker is the chance of drawing all seven cards in my example win line by turn 6. The deck doesn't need all seven, because each part has backups.

I only run 3 Sackville-Bagginses because it's legendary, and a second copy can still be sacrificed to Zealot.

The sideboard is aimed at the decks the meta shows: discard against control and Dimir, and graveyard hate against Reanimator. It also has extra removal for Prowess and Landfall.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Gideon's Memorial, Solitary Cell and Ajani Unrelenting.
results.text:
I built a Boros (red-white) Superfriends deck, meaning one that wins through several planeswalkers at once, with a token army to protect them. No published list in the past 400 days runs these three cards together, so this is an untested brew.

**Three directions I considered:**
1. **Boros Dragons with Ajani on top.** Borrow the Dragons creatures (Sarkhan, Momo, Magda). The problem: Ajani Unrelenting's −3 deals 4 damage to every creature except your tokens, so it would kill your own Dragons.
2. **Jeskai Control.** Run Ajani as the finisher behind Lightning Helix and sweepers. That leaves Gideon's Memorial with nothing to do, since its mana only casts planeswalkers and its bonus only helps tokens.
3. **Boros Superfriends tokens (chosen).** I picked this one because it's the only direction where all three cards do real work.

**How the three cards fit together:**
- **Gideon's Memorial:** Its mana only casts planeswalkers, so it works as ramp: turn 2 Memorial puts a 4-mana walker out on turn 3 and Ajani Unrelenting out on turn 5. It also gives your tokens +1/+0 and vigilance, so they can attack and still guard your planeswalkers.
- **Ajani Unrelenting:** It makes a 2/2 Cadet token every time you use any loyalty ability. With Elspeth, Storm Slayer out, every token you make comes in doubled, so that's two Cadets each time. Your creatures are almost all tokens, which makes its −3 a one-sided board wipe.
- **Solitary Cell:** It's 2-mana removal for anything costing 3 or less. Late in the game, it turns spare legendary cards into new draws. Every planeswalker and Memorial in the deck is legendary (16 cards).

**The plan:** Interact early with Burst Lightning, Get Lost, Lightning Helix and Solitary Cell. Then use Memorial to cast planeswalkers ahead of schedule: Ajani, Outland Chaperone, Chandra, Elspeth, and finally Ajani Unrelenting. Antiquities on the Loose and the planeswalkers build a token board. Ajani Unrelenting's −3 clears the opponent's creatures while your tokens survive, and his +1 gives everything haste to finish the game.

**About the odds:** The checker says you'll have drawn every card in the listed win sequence by turn 7 in only 3.2% of games. The deck doesn't need the exact sequence, though: any Memorial plus any two or three planeswalkers gets you there.

**Other notes:**
- The mana base (24 lands) and the cheap removal come from Boros Dragons lists. You have 17 white and 16 red sources, a bit less red than Dragons lists run (about 19). The Memorial helps make up for it when casting Ajani Unrelenting, which needs two red mana.
- I'm running 3 copies of Ajani Unrelenting, not 4. It costs 6, and extra copies can be discarded to Solitary Cell anyway.
- I left out Clarion Conqueror, a common Boros card, on purpose: it stops activated abilities, including your own planeswalkers'.
- The 15-card sideboard is aimed at the current top decks: Seam Rip, Pyroclasm, Rest in Peace, Dawn's Truce, Quintorius Kand, plus one more Get Lost and two more Chandras.

results.prompt: Brew me a Pioneer deck built around Slumbering Trudge, Fight Rigging and The Great Henge.
results.text:
I built **Mono-Green Ferocious Stompy**, a brew. No published deck runs these three cards together. Slumbering Trudge's real home is Modern's Fanatic Eldrazi deck, which uses it the same way. That deck depends on cards that aren't legal in Pioneer, so I kept its idea and rebuilt the shell from Pioneer cards.

**The plan:** If you cast Slumbering Trudge for X=0, it's a 6/6 for one green mana. It enters tapped with stun counters, so it can't attack for a few turns, but every effect that checks power counts it right away:
- **The Great Henge** costs only {1}{G}{G} with Trudge out (two green with a 7-power creature).
- **Fight Rigging** adds a counter at the start of combat, making Trudge 7/7, so you play the hidden card for free every turn.
- **Raucous Audience** taps for GG once you control a 4-power creature.
- **Ghalta** drops to GG once your creatures add up to 10 power.

From there, Henge draws a card off every creature you cast. Fight Rigging's hidden card is often a big payoff (Ghalta, Craterhoof, another Henge or Turntimber Symbiosis), and you win with Ghalta or Craterhoof. Hunter's Talent is the main-deck removal: Trudge deals 6 damage with it even while tapped.

**How I chose:** I considered three directions:
1. Mono-green ramp using the dork, Badgermole Cub and Ouroboroid package from Selesnya Company and Mono-Green Devotion.
2. Selesnya Company, since Collected Company can hit Trudge (mana value 1).
3. Golgari, adding Fatal Push and Thoughtseize.

I picked mono-green because it runs the most cheap power and the most mana creatures. That's exactly what all three of your cards reward. Company can't find Henge or Fight Rigging, and black would only add interaction, not a faster engine.

**Odds:** You'll have Trudge or Ouroboroid plus Fight Rigging or Henge by turn 3 about 51% of the time (75% for a power enabler alone). The full winning line drawn in exact order is rare, but you only need that core pair.

**Assumptions:** No budget limit. 21 lands: 17 Forests, Boseiju, Lair of the Hydra and 2 Turntimber Symbiosis that can be played as lands. That's in line with Mono-Green Devotion lists. The sideboard is aimed at the top decks right now: Ram Through, graveyard hate, artifact/enchantment removal, Surrak against removal-heavy decks, and Tamiyo's Safekeeping to protect Trudge.

--- After review ---
I followed the reviewer's diagnosis but changed half of the suggested fix. The resubmitted deck was accepted with no warnings.

- **Cut both Outcaster Trailblazers.** The reviewer is right. Its draw only triggers on creatures with 4+ power entering, and the dorks and Ouroboroid enter too small. That leaves it as a one-shot ramp 3-drop fighting The Great Henge and Fight Rigging for the turn-3 slot.
- **Added a 4th Raucous Audience.** It taps for GG whenever you control a creature with 4+ power, so next to a turn-2 Trudge it's a steady ramp piece.
- **Added a 2nd Ulvenwald Oddity instead of a 4th The Great Henge.** The Great Henge is legendary, so a 4th copy would often be a dead draw. Oddity is a 4/4 trample haste creature. It makes Henge cheaper, draws a card off Henge when it enters, turns on Audience's GG, and late in the game it can transform to give the team +1/+1, trample and haste.

The win line hasn't changed:
1. Turn 1: a mana dork.
2. Turn 2: Slumbering Trudge for one mana (X=0), plus Raucous Audience.
3. Turn 3: The Great Henge for 3 mana, then Fight Rigging. Fight Rigging's counter makes Trudge 7/7, which lets you play the hidden card for free.
4. Finish with Ghalta for GG and Craterhoof Behemoth.

**How often it happens:** the deck check found that you'll have drawn every card in that exact line by turn 5 in only about 0.1% of games. That's mostly because there's only one Craterhoof and the check doesn't count cards drawn from Henge or hidden by Fight Rigging. Expect the turn-5 kill only when the draws line up. In most games you'll win with Trudge, Ghalta and Ouroboroid boards instead of the full sequence.

results.prompt: Brew me a Pioneer deck built around Guiding Voice, Practiced Offense and Favored Hoplite.
results.text:
This is an Azorius Heroic brew: 18 lands, 16 creatures and 26 cheap spells that target your own creatures. On turn 1 you play Favored Hoplite. Each spell that targets it gives it a +1/+1 counter and stops all damage to it that turn. Guiding Voice costs one white and puts two counters on it: its own counter plus the heroic one.

**How it wins:** Phalanx Leader puts a counter on every creature you control whenever you target it. Practiced Offense then puts a counter on each of your creatures, triggers heroic again on whatever it targets, and gives that creature double strike. Next turn you can flash it back for {1}{W}. The aim is to win around turn 4–5 with one or two big, protected attackers.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Mono-White heroic.** Seasoned Hallowblade, Lagonna-Band Trailblazer and Professor of Symbology. The only two real lists running all three of your cards are this deck.
2. **Boros.** Monstrous Rage and Reckless Rage borrowed from the Prowess decks on the menu.
3. **Azorius Heroic.** Used in 3 recent lists, which all play 4 Favored Hoplite. I chose this one because its blue spells protect the creature you build up: Slip Out the Back, Shore Up and Stormchaser Drake. That matters a lot against Fatal Push, Golgari and Dimir.

**How Guiding Voice's Learn works here:** When you cast it, you can take a Lesson card from your sideboard and put it into your hand. Five of the 15 sideboard slots are Lessons:
- Enter the Avatar State: flying, first strike, lifelink and hexproof for one white mana, and it triggers heroic.
- Octopus Form: protection, and it also triggers heroic.
- Reduce to Memory and Airbender's Reversal: removal.
- Academic Probation: stops a key card for a turn.

When you don't need a Lesson, Learn lets you discard a card to draw one instead.

**Things to know:**
- **Only 3 Practiced Offense.** Flashback means each copy can be cast twice. More copies would clog hands in a deck whose cards average 1.5 mana.
- **18 lands.** That's below the 19.5 the Azorius Heroic lists run. I dropped their green adventure creature (Elusive Otter), so there's less to spend mana on.
- **12 blue sources.** That's below their roughly 15, but this version has fewer blue cards.
- **Odds.** By turn 2 you have at least one heroic-style creature and one targeting spell in about 92% of games (no mulligans). The listed line with those exact cards (Hoplite, Guiding Voice, Phalanx Leader, Practiced Offense) only comes together by turn 5 in about 5% of games. In practice, any of the 16 creatures plus any of the 26 targeting spells plays out the same way.

results.prompt: Brew me a Pioneer deck built around Jeskai Revelation, Inevitable Defeat and Tablet of Discovery.
results.text:
I built a four-color control brew. It ramps into Jeskai Revelation with Tablet of Discovery and uses Inevitable Defeat as removal you can't counter that also drains 3 life.

**Three directions I considered:**
1. **Port the Standard 4C Control deck.** played_with showed that all 135 real lists running these three cards together are one Standard deck: 4C Control, built on Tablet, Stock Up, Consult the Star Charts, Flashback and Revelation.
2. **Take the UW Control package from the menu** (No More Lies, The Wandering Emperor, Teferi) and splash red and black. I dropped this because Tablet's RR can only pay for instants and sorceries, so planeswalkers waste the ramp.
3. **Use a Lessons/Izzet Tablet shell** (Pioneer Lessons decks already play Tablet). I dropped this because a fast tempo deck can't support a 7-mana, three-color spell or a four-color mana base.

**I chose direction 1** because it's the only one where every card in the deck can spend Tablet's mana. I still kept the menu's UW Control interaction: No More Lies, Get Lost, Consult the Star Charts and Supreme Verdict.

**The plan:** Play Tablet on turn 3. From then on it taps for RR that only instants and sorceries can use, so you have 6 mana for spells on turn 4 and 7 on turn 5.
- **Before that:** Fiery Impulse, Lightning Helix, Get Lost, No More Lies and the sweepers (Supreme Verdict, Deafening Clarion) keep you alive.
- **Jeskai Revelation** answers a threat, deals 4 damage, makes two Monks, draws 2 cards and gains 4 life.
- **Flashback** casts a Revelation again from the graveyard, and Tablet's RR can pay that cost.
- **Inevitable Defeat** exiles their best permanent and drains 3.

You win by stacking Revelation damage, Monk attacks, Defeat drains and Helix, usually around turn 8.

**Mana:** The deck runs 27 lands to cast the 7-drop. Triomes, shocklands and 3 Great Hall of the Biblioplex (which makes any color for instants and sorceries, at 1 life each) give 16 white, 21 blue, 16 red and 9 black sources by check_deck's count. The deck passed check_deck with no warnings.

**Honest odds:**
- You'll have Tablet in your opening hand or first two draws about 49% of the time, and a Stock Up or Consult about 70%.
- You'll have seen a Revelation by turn 6 about 60% of the time, before counting what Stock Up and Consult dig up.
- This is a slow control deck. Its worst matchups are likely fast aggro (Mono-Red Prowess) and decks that attack your hand early (Golgari Midrange).

The sideboard targets the decks at the top of the menu:
- **Rest in Peace** against Greasefang and Izzet Phoenix.
- **Dovin's Veto, Duress and Mystical Dispute** against control.
- **High Noon, Temporary Lockdown, Sear, the extra Clarion and Erode** against Prowess and midrange.

--- After review ---
I resubmitted the deck with no card changes.

**Flag 1, Savai Triome: kept.** The reviewer's premise was wrong. The card lookup shows Savai Triome is a Mountain Plains Swamp that taps for {R}, {W} or {B}, not green. So it already makes black, and it's one of only two lands here that can pay for all three of Inevitable Defeat's colours (Godless Shrine can't make red). Raffine's Tower makes {W}{U}{B} and can't make red, so swapping it in would be a step down for Defeat.

Black sources stay at 7: Savai Triome, Raffine's Tower, 2 Xander's Lounge, Watery Grave, Godless Shrine and Multiversal Passage. That's enough for the deck's only black card, a 4-mana spell it runs three copies of.

The win line and the 60 cards are unchanged, and the submission was accepted with no warnings. The checker did report that all six cards in the win line are drawn by turn 7 in only 1.2% of games. That figure needs every piece drawn and doesn't count Stock Up or Consult the Star Charts digging, so the real odds are higher, but the full line will come together less often than its turn-7 target suggests.

results.prompt: Brew me a Pioneer deck built around Tolarian Terror, Bushwhack and Eddymurk Crab.
results.text:
I built a Simic (blue-green) "Big Serpents" deck. It's a brew: no published list in the last 400 days plays all three of your cards together.

**The plan:** On turns 1–3 you cast cheap instants and sorceries: Consider, Opt, Sleight of Hand, Spell Pierce, and Bushwhack in its land-search mode. Each one in your graveyard makes Tolarian Terror and Eddymurk Crab cost {1} less, so they often land on turn 3–4 for 1–3 mana as 5/5s. Terror has ward 2. Crab has flash and taps two creatures when it enters, which clears blockers or freezes attackers. Once you have a 5/5, Bushwhack's fight mode and Tail Swipe become 1-mana removal. Tail Swipe is an instant, and in your main phase it gives your creature +1/+1 before the fight. Snakeskin Veil protects your threat, and two 5/5s finish the game in a few swings.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Simic tempo**, with Bushwhack and Tail Swipe fighting alongside the big creatures. This is the one I chose.
2. **Izzet Crab with a green splash**, borrowing that deck's burn and its 21-land mana.
3. **Sultai**, adding Fatal Push and Thoughtseize from the Golgari and Dimir decks on the menu.

I picked Simic because Bushwhack is green and only works as removal next to big creatures. Simic also adds a second fight spell and gives clean two-colour mana without stretching for three colours.

**What I borrowed:**
- **Stormchaser's Talent** (in 16.9% of recent lists) from the Izzet Prowess / Lessons package. It's an early blocker, and you can level it up later to get back a spent spell.
- **Serpent of the Pass:** two copies as a third cost-reducing 5/5. It counts any noncreature, nonland card in your graveyard, so Stormchaser's Talent helps too.
- **Mana and cantrips:** the cantrip core and land count are based on the Izzet Crab list that went 4-2 in the May 17 Challenge.

**Two deliberate choices:**
- **Removal:** the deck checker flagged Rapid Hybridization and Tail Swipe as rarely played. I cut Hybridization from 3 to 2 and added 1 Boomerang Basics. I kept the rest because Hybridization kills Sheoldred or Greasefang for 1 mana before you have a 5/5, and Tail Swipe is what turns your big creatures into permanent removal.
- **20 lands**, while the checker recommended 23.6. That number is inflated because it counts your 7-drops at full cost. In practice they cost 1–3, and almost every other spell costs 1.

**Odds:** By turn 4 on the play, you'll have one of the 10 big creatures 86% of the time, a fight spell 74% of the time, and both 63% of the time.

**Sideboard:** It's aimed at the top decks on the menu:
- **Greasefang:** Soul-Guide Lantern and Unlicensed Hearse.
- **Mono-Red Prowess:** Aether Gust and Essence Scatter.
- **UW Control:** Negate and Mystical Dispute.
- **Parhelion and Unholy Annex:** Pick Your Poison.

--- After review ---
I took the reviewer's fix as given.

**What changed:**
- **Removed 4 Stormchaser's Talent.** It's an enchantment, so it never goes into the graveyard as an instant or sorcery and never makes Tolarian Terror or Eddymurk Crab cheaper. Its level 2 also takes an instant or sorcery back out of the graveyard, which makes Serpent of the Pass cost more. It's played mostly in Izzet Prowess (369 of its 570 recent lists), where prowess creatures reward casting spells. This deck has nothing like that.
- **Added 2 Fading Hope.** It's a 1-mana instant that returns a creature to its owner's hand and lets you scry 1 if that creature cost 3 or less. It clears a blocker or slows down an attacker, and it fills the graveyard.
- **Added 2 Spell Pierce, for 4 total.** Every 1-mana spell in the early turns now also makes the threats cheaper.

**Why it's better:** The deck now has 30 instants and sorceries instead of 28. Every early card goes into the graveyard to make your threats cheaper. Fading Hope also works well with Eddymurk Crab: the Crab taps two blockers and Fading Hope removes a third, so the 5/5s can attack.

**About the numbers:** The deck passed with no warnings and is still exactly 60 cards. The tool says you'll have drawn every single card in the win line by turn 7 in only 0.4% of games. You don't need all of them, though. Any 5/5 plus a way past blockers or removal does the job, so that figure badly understates how often the deck actually wins.

results.prompt: Brew me a Pioneer deck built around Lorehold, the Historian, Sarkhan, Dragon Ascendant and Shivan Devastator.
results.text:
I built this as a **Boros Dragons brew**. There's no published list in any format running all three of your cards together. Two of them, Lorehold and Sarkhan, show up together in Standard's Boros Dragons (all 8 recent Lorehold lists are Boros Dragons), so I took that deck's structure and mana and upgraded it with Pioneer cards.

**How it wins:** 17 Dragon cards make Sarkhan reliable: turn 2, reveal a Dragon from your hand and get a Treasure. Momo makes your first flier each turn cost 1 less, so the best start is:
- **Turn 1:** Momo.
- **Turn 2:** Sarkhan, revealing a Dragon for the Treasure.
- **Turn 3:** Lorehold for 4 mana (3 lands plus the Treasure). It's a 5/5 flier with haste, so it attacks right away.
- **Turns 4–5:** Shivan Devastator with all your spare mana in X. Momo's discount effectively adds 1 to X, and every Dragon that enters grows Sarkhan.

Lorehold also does two things on the opponent's upkeep. You can discard a card to draw one, which gets rid of extra copies of legends. And any instant you draw that turn can be cast for 2 mana through miracle, so a Burst Lightning or Helix comes at instant speed and cheap. Goldspan Dragon makes your Treasures produce two mana each, which feeds Devastator's X.

**Why this direction:** I considered three:
1. **Boros Dragons with Pioneer upgrades.** Goldspan Dragon, Glorybringer and Invasion of Tarkir were added on top of the Standard shell. This is the one I chose, because it's the only direction where all three of your cards help each other: Sarkhan reveals the other two, Momo discounts both, and Lorehold casts your burn for 2.
2. **Mono-red using the Prowess deck's burn and creatures** (Burst Lightning, Screaming Nemesis). Rejected because Lorehold needs white.
3. **Boros miracle control around Lorehold.** Rejected because it sidelines Sarkhan and Devastator.

**Things to know:**
- **Odds:** you draw Lorehold by turn 5 in about 46% of games with 3 copies, so I ran 4 even though it's legendary (Lorehold's own loot gets rid of a duplicate). Sarkhan in your opening 8 cards is about 45%. The exact turn-3 Lorehold start needs Momo, Sarkhan and Lorehold all together, which is rare. Normally you'll be casting 5-mana hasty fliers on turns 4–5.
- **24 lands:** the checker compared me to Boros Aggro, which plays about 20. I kept 24 on purpose: the deck has 11 five-drops and an X spell, and Standard Boros Dragons also runs 24.
- **Two flagged cards I kept:** the checker noted that Invasion of Tarkir and Magmatic Hellkite almost never appear in Pioneer decks. I kept them because they help the Dragon plan:
  - **Invasion of Tarkir:** 3–5 damage for 2 mana, growing with each Dragon you reveal from your hand.
  - **Magmatic Hellkite:** a Dragon flier that destroys one of the opponent's nonbasic lands. Most Pioneer mana bases are full of those.
- **Clarion Conqueror is sideboard only:** it shuts off your own Treasures and Goldspan. It comes in against Greasefang (it stops Parhelion from crewing) and Cauldron.
- **The rest of the sideboard** targets the top decks: Rest in Peace, Magebane Lizard and Brotherhood's End against Prowess and other graveyard and spell decks, and Exorcise and Lithomantic Barrage against Golgari and UW Control.

results.prompt: Brew me a Modern deck built around Eyetwitch, Stitcher's Supplier and Flare of Malice.
results.text:
I built this as a **Rakdos Reanimator brew**. Eyetwitch is the new piece, and it gives the deck a second way to throw Archon of Cruelty into the graveyard.

**How it wins:** Play a black 1-drop, then sacrifice it to Flare of Malice so you don't pay Flare's 4 mana. Flare makes the opponent sacrifice their biggest creature or planeswalker. When Eyetwitch dies it lets you "learn": discard Archon to draw a card, or grab a Lesson from your sideboard. Stitcher's Supplier mills 3 cards when it enters and again when it dies. Then Persist brings Archon back on turn 2–4. Archon makes them sacrifice a creature, discard and lose 3 life every time it enters or attacks, and it draws you a card and gains you 3 life. Bloodghast and Phoenix keep coming back from the graveyard, so you can win even when you never find Archon.

**Three directions I considered:**
1. **Rakdos Reanimator (chosen).** Real decks already run Supplier and Flare together, mostly in Reanimator (24 lists) and Grixis Persist (24 lists). Eyetwitch fits that shell: it's another black creature Flare can sacrifice, and its learn trigger is a free discard.
2. **Grixis Persist with Psychic Frog.** This is the version on the menu, but adding blue weakens the black/red mana that Bloodghast and Flare need.
3. **Rakdos sacrifice deck with Goblin Bombardment (from the Energy list).** It uses the creatures well, but it doesn't have a strong finisher like Archon.

I chose the first because it's the only one where all three cards push the same plan.

**Changes to the proven list** (a recent 4-3 Modern Challenge list):
- **Added:** 4 Eyetwitch.
- **Cut:** 2 Voldaren Epicure and 2 Orcish Bowmasters. Both Bowmasters moved to the sideboard, which is where most Reanimator lists play them (88%).
- **Unchanged:** the 17-land mana base. The archetype averages about 18 lands, but with 23 one-drops and 4 Faithless Looting, 17 works.

**Sideboard:** It's mostly the usual Reanimator sideboard. I added three Lessons that Eyetwitch can fetch: Firebending Lesson, Iroh's Demonstration (both good against Energy and Prowess creatures) and Dai Li Indoctrination (hand disruption against combo). I left out Vexing Bauble on purpose: it would counter your own free Flare.

**Odds:** Without a mulligan, you'll have Persist plus a card that fills your graveyard (Looting, Supplier or Eyetwitch) by turn 3 about 42% of the time. In other games you play a slower game with Flare, removal and the creatures that come back.

--- After review ---
I took the reviewer's fix: both Detective's Phoenix are out and 2 Thoughtseize are in. The deck is still 60 cards and was accepted with no warnings.

- **Why Phoenix went:** It can only come back from the graveyard through its bestow cost, which means paying {R} and exiling cards worth 6+ mana value from your graveyard. In this deck the easiest card to exile for that is Archon of Cruelty, the card Persist needs to bring back. Hollow One decks have cheap filler to exile instead; this deck doesn't. So the backup plan was fighting the main plan.
- **Why Thoughtseize:** It costs one black mana, so it fits easily in turns 1–2. It strips away the counterspell or graveyard hate that would stop the Persist on Archon. It also shows up in 146 recent Grixis Persist lists, the shell this deck borrows from.

The main plan hasn't changed. Eyetwitch or Stitcher's Supplier gets sacrificed to cast Flare of Malice for free, which puts Archon in the graveyard (Eyetwitch through its discard-to-draw death ability, Supplier through its mill). Then Persist brings Archon back on turn 2–3.

The submit check says all six cards in the win line are drawn by turn 3 in only 0.2% of games. That number is misleading: the line doesn't need all six cards. It needs one way to get Archon into the graveyard, plus Persist, plus Archon itself.

results.prompt: Brew me a Modern deck built around Fight Rigging, Turntimber Symbiosis and Slumbering Trudge.
results.text:
I built a mono-green big-creature deck, and it's a brew. The three cards work well together. Slumbering Trudge is a 6/6 for one mana if you cast it with X=0. It enters stunned, but Fight Rigging doesn't need it to attack. Rigging's counter at the start of combat makes Trudge a 7/7, and having a 7-power creature lets you play the card Rigging hid for free. The best things to hide are Turntimber Symbiosis, The Great Henge or Craterhoof Behemoth.

**The plan:** On turn 1, cast Trudge for X=0, or cast Green Sun's Zenith for X=0 to put it into play. That gives you 8 ways to get a turn-1 6/6, since Trudge counts as a 1-mana-value card everywhere except the stack. On turn 2, play Fanatic of Rhonas, which taps for four green mana once Trudge is out. On turn 3, play Rigging and get your hidden card free. Turntimber Symbiosis put into play from Rigging can find a second Trudge as a 9/9, because cheap creatures get three extra counters. Ouroboroid and Rigging keep adding counters every turn. You win around turn 5, usually with Craterhoof, which you can find with Zenith off the big mana from Fanatic and Badgermole Cub. Ram Through doubles as removal, since your creatures hit very hard.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Mono-green stompy (chosen).** This is the shell the real Trudge lists use: Fanatic, Ouroboroid, Zenith and Great Henge. Every card in it pushes power to 7 or uses that power.
2. **Borrowing the Eldrazi Ramp package from the menu** (Utopia Sprawl, Sowing Mycospawn, Emrakul hidden under Rigging). It ramps well, but Trudge and Turntimber don't add much there.
3. **A Neoform / Summoner's Pact combo shell.** It's faster, but it pushes all three of your cards into the background.

I picked option 1 because it's the only one where all three of your cards are doing the main work.

**Things to know:**
- **Turntimber is mostly a land.** It's usually a land you can play untapped by paying 3 life, and only sometimes a free 7-mana spell. The checker counts 17 lands because it leaves out the 4 Turntimbers. With them it's 19, plus 12 mana creatures.
- **Odds:** You see Trudge or Zenith by turn 3 in about 75% of games. Seeing both that and Rigging by turn 3 happens about 35% of the time, so many games are a fast stompy start with Rigging as a bonus.
- **Matchups:** Interaction is light. Energy's Galvanic Discharge and the decks that remove big creatures are the hardest matchups.
- **Sideboard:** It's aimed at Affinity, Amulet and the graveyard decks: Ouphe, Force of Vigor, Endurance, Pick Your Poison and Beast Within.

results.prompt: Brew me a Legacy deck built around Riddlesmith, Ovalchase Daredevil and Echo of Eons.
results.text:
I built a Dimir artifact brew where Riddlesmith's looting fuels Ovalchase Daredevil and Echo of Eons. No published deck in the last 400 days runs all three of your cards together, so there's no proven list behind this.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Affinity package from the menu:** Mox Opal, Lotus Petal, Baubles, Emry, Urza's Saga and Kappa Cannoneer, with Riddlesmith and Daredevil added as a card-draw engine.
2. **Hullbreacher Stompy's Echo package:** this is where Echo of Eons actually shows up with artifacts in Legacy. Hullbreacher or Narset makes Echo one-sided.
3. **Grixis artifact storm** with Grapeshot.

**What I chose:** I combined 1 and 2. The Affinity base supplies the artifacts that Riddlesmith needs, and Hullbreacher turns Echo from a symmetrical refill into a win.

**How it works:**
- **The engine:** Riddlesmith lets you draw and then discard whenever you cast an artifact.
  - Discard Ovalchase Daredevil to the loot. When the artifact resolves and enters, Daredevil returns to your hand. With both out, every Bauble, Petal, Mox Opal or Emry recast is a free card.
  - Discard Echo of Eons to the same loot and flash it back for {2}{U} instead of paying 6.
- **The win:** Cast Hullbreacher (it has flash, and Ancient Tomb helps get it out early), then flash back Echo.
  - You draw a fresh seven. The opponent's seven draws turn into seven Treasures for you, so they end with an empty hand.
  - Kappa Cannoneer grows and gets unblockable as all those artifacts enter. Urza's Saga constructs and Daredevil beats help finish.
- **Narset:** one copy, as a second way to make Echo one-sided.
- **Backup outlet:** Currency Converter is a second discard outlet that Urza's Saga can fetch.
- **Mana and sideboard:** The mana base is close to Affinity's (16 lands, 16 blue sources). The sideboard targets the menu's top decks: Tempo, Tron, Sneak and Show, Oops and Ocelot.

**Odds:**
- By turn 3 you have both Riddlesmith and Echo about 22% of the time. Counting Converter as an outlet, you have an outlet plus Echo about 33% of the time.
- The checker says the whole six-card line is fully drawn by turn 5 in only 0.4% of games. That number is low partly because it counts every card in the line, including Lotus Petal and Kappa Cannoneer, which aren't strictly required, and it doesn't count Emry's mill-4 or the deck's extra draw.
- The other games play out as a fast artifact beatdown deck backed by Force of Will.

--- After review ---
I took the reviewer's fix: **−3 Currency Converter, +3 Chromatic Star**. The deck is resubmitted and accepted, still 60 cards and legal.

**Why:** The reviewer was right. Currency Converter's loot costs {2} and taps, which repeats what Riddlesmith already does for free. Its exile trigger also works against the deck, because Echo of Eons and Ovalchase Daredevil need to stay in the graveyard. Chromatic Star keeps the one useful thing Converter offered, a 1-mana artifact to cast, and does more with it:
- **Engine:** casting it triggers Riddlesmith, and it entering the battlefield brings Daredevil back to hand.
- **Card draw:** it draws a card when it goes to the graveyard, so it replaces itself.
- **Mana:** it makes any color, which helps cast Daredevil.
- **Recasting:** Emry can cast it again from the graveyard, giving another loot and another card.
- **Saga:** Urza's Saga can still fetch it.

**Unchanged:** the rest of the main deck, the sideboard and the plan.

**Odds:** The tool says the full 7-card line is all drawn by turn 4 in only about 0.1% of games. That number doesn't count the deck's own card draw (Riddlesmith loots, Baubles, Star, the Echo refill), so it's a worst case. Still, the deck doesn't need every piece: it wins whenever the Riddlesmith artifact engine plus an Echo flashback comes together, and the Hullbreacher punish makes that much stronger.

results.prompt: Brew me a Legacy deck built around Arclight Phoenix, Buried Alive and Flow State.
results.text:
I built a Grixis "Phoenix Ritual" combo brew. No published list in the last 400 days plays Arclight Phoenix, Buried Alive and Flow State together. The only list pairing Phoenix with Buried Alive was a Modern rogue deck built on rituals and Faithless Looting, so I used that idea.

**How it wins:** Dark Ritual (instant) gives BBB for Buried Alive (sorcery), which puts three Phoenixes in the graveyard. A third spell, such as Unmask cast for free by exiling a black card, triggers all three Phoenixes at the start of combat. They come back with haste and fly in for 9, as early as turn 1. On later turns they keep attacking. Cabal Therapy's flashback lets you sacrifice a Phoenix after combat, which puts it back in the graveyard and counts as another spell. The target is a kill by turn 3.

**What each requested card does:**
- **Phoenix:** the win condition. Its check is "three or more instants and sorceries this turn", so 32 of the 46 non-land cards are instants or sorceries costing 0–2 that count toward it.
- **Buried Alive:** fills the graveyard with three Phoenixes at once. Dark Ritual and Lotus Petal (8 total) let you cast it on turn 1–2 with mana left over. Faithless Looting and Careful Study are the backup way to discard Phoenixes.
- **Flow State:** a sorcery that counts toward the three spells and digs for the pieces. It's almost always the upgraded version (keep two cards), since Ritual, Brainstorm, Looting and Thoughtseize put an instant and a sorcery in your graveyard early.

**Three directions I considered:**
1. Izzet Tempo's cantrip-and-counter shell with a black splash. Too slow and too light on mana for a 3-mana Buried Alive.
2. Reanimator's fast-mana package (Dark Ritual, Lotus Petal, Thoughtseize, Cabal Therapy, Unmask, Looting), plus blue for Flow State, Brainstorm, Ponder and Force of Will. **This is the one I picked**, because Ritual into Buried Alive into one more spell is the only line that gets three Phoenixes attacking on turns 1–2.
3. A real Reanimator hybrid (Buried Alive for Phoenix plus Griselbrand). That splits the deck between two plans.

**Things to know:**
- Entomb and Gitaxian Probe would fit perfectly, but both are banned in Legacy, so Faithless Looting and Careful Study handle discarding Phoenixes instead.
- The deck has 15 black sources, while real Reanimator lists average about 18. That's because 12 of my 14 lands and fetches also need to make red for Looting and blue for the cantrips.
- The tool shows only about a 0.4% chance of drawing every specific card in the win line by turn 3. That number doesn't account for Brainstorm, Ponder and Flow State digging, and the deck has many other ways to reach three spells. Still, expect a real mix of turn-2 explosions and slower games.
- Orcish Bowmasters and graveyard hate are the main threats. The sideboard has Abrade and Pyroblast for those, plus Fatal Push and Lightning Bolt for Ocelot Aggro.

results.prompt: Brew me a Pauper deck built around Ardent Recruit, Search Party Captain and Springleaf Drum.
results.text:
I built a white "artifact weenie" brew (go-wide small creatures). It takes the creatures and interaction from the format's Mono-White Aggro deck and puts a base of artifacts underneath them.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Mono-White Aggro with artifacts (chosen):** Thraben Inspector, Novice Inspector, Kor Skyfisher, Battle Screech, Prismatic Strands and Thraben Charm from the menu, plus artifact lands and Glint Hawk.
2. **Boros artifacts:** Glint Hawk, Galvanic Blast and Lightning Bolt, using Springleaf Drum to fix red.
3. **White Affinity:** Frogmite, Myr Enforcer and Ornithopter.

I picked the first one because Battle Screech is the best way to attack with lots of creatures at once, which is exactly what Search Party Captain wants. The Clue tokens and Ancient Dens also count toward Ardent Recruit's metalcraft (3+ artifacts) without making the deck weaker.

**What each requested card does here:**
- **Ardent Recruit** is a 3/3 for one mana once you control three artifacts. 22 cards help with that: 4 Ancient Den, 3 Rustvale Bridge, 4 Springleaf Drum, 3 Ornithopter, and 8 Inspectors (each makes a Clue token, which is an artifact).
- **Springleaf Drum** is a third artifact for one mana. It turns your cheap creatures into mana, even ones that just came into play, and it's a cheap thing for Glint Hawk or Kor Skyfisher to return to your hand.
- **Search Party Captain** is the refill. It costs one less for each creature you attacked with, so after an attack with three or four creatures (often Battle Screech birds) you cast it after combat for W or for free and draw a card.

**The plan:** On turns 1 and 2, play Ancient Den, an Inspector and Drum, then cast a 3/3 Recruit. On turn 3, cast Battle Screech, then flash it back by tapping three white creatures for four flying birds total. On turn 4, swing wide and cast Captain afterward. That should win around turn 5. Prismatic Strands and Thraben Charm protect the board against Madness and fight blockers.

**Odds, honestly:**
- Drawing every specific card in that exact line by turn 5 happens only about 2% of the time. The real deck relies on swapping in copies: 27 creatures, 22 artifact sources, 8 four-drop payoffs.
- Seeing at least one Den, one Clue-maker and one Drum or Ornithopter by turn 3 is about 33%. That undercounts metalcraft, since two Dens plus a Clue also works.

**Other notes:**
- Pauper allows only 4 Ancient Den, so the 3 Rustvale Bridges fill in as extra artifact lands. They enter tapped, but they're indestructible.
- No published list in the last 400 days plays these three cards together, so this is untested.
- The 15-card sideboard leaves out Dust to Dust, the usual artifact-removal card for this shell, because it would also hit your own lands. Revoke Existence and Destroy Evil cover that role instead.

--- After review ---
I made the reviewer's suggested fix: all 3 Ornithopter are out and 3 Lunarch Veteran are in. Nothing else in the main deck or sideboard changed, and the deck was accepted at exactly 60 cards.

**Why:** Ornithopter has 0 power and isn't white. It added nothing to the attack and couldn't help pay to flash back Battle Screech or Prismatic Strands, since both need white creatures tapped. The deck already has plenty of artifacts for Ardent Recruit's 3+ artifact bonus: 7 artifact lands, 4 Springleaf Drum, and 12 cards that make or return artifacts (the two Inspectors and Glint Hawk). So Ornithopter's only job was already covered.

**What Lunarch Veteran does:** It's a white one-drop with 1 power. It can be tapped to flash back both spells, it attacks to help make Search Party Captain cheaper, and it's another body to tap with Drum. It also gains 1 life whenever another creature of yours enters, which adds up with Battle Screech tokens. Later it can come back from the graveyard as a 1/1 flier for 1W.

**Why not Guardians' Pledge:** It's a reasonable finisher, but it doesn't add a body. Bodies are what pay for the flashbacks and make Captain cheaper.

**The kill turn:** The game plan is the same. I submitted it as finishing on turn 5. That's one turn later than my turn-by-turn plan, because the turn-4 attack still has to deal its damage. Drawing every card in that exact sequence by turn 5 happens in only about 2% of games, mulligans included. The deck has lots of interchangeable early creatures and artifacts, so in practice it wins through many versions of this line, not just that exact one.

results.prompt: Brew me a Pauper deck built around Aurora Eidolon, Sandstorm Eidolon and Spirit Mascot.
results.text:
This is a Boros (red-white) graveyard-recursion brew. I tried three directions:
- **Synthesizer artifact package** (Kor Skyfisher, Glint Hawk, Lembas): rejected. It has too few multicolored spells, so the Eidolons would rarely come back.
- **Three or more colors** for more gold cards: rejected. The mana gets worse.
- **Boros multicolored-spell recursion, borrowing Faithless Looting and Lightning Bolt from the Madness package:** chosen. It's the only one where nearly every creature you cast brings the Eidolons back.

**How it plays:** Faithless Looting, Thrilling Discovery and Pursue the Past let you throw Aurora Eidolon and Sandstorm Eidolon away early as fuel. After that, 20 multicolored cards (Spirit Mascot, Stonebound Mentor, Battlegate Mimic, Boros Recruit and the two gold draw spells) return them to your hand whenever you cast one.

**How it wins:** Each time an Eidolon returns, a flashback is cast, or Relic of Progenitus exiles one of your own cards, Spirit Mascot gets a +1/+1 counter. Stonebound Mentor also lets you scry 1 each time. Then you spend the Eidolons over and over:
- Sacrifice Sandstorm Eidolon (pay R) so their best blocker can't block the big Mascot.
- Sacrifice Aurora Eidolon (pay W) to prevent 3 damage and save Mascot from a Bolt or a bad block.

Lightning Bolt and Firebolt clear the way and deal the last points. The target is to kill around turn 6.

**About the odds and the checker:**
- The 0.2% the checker reported is the chance of drawing all 8 cards in the win line by turn 6. That isn't how the deck actually works. It only needs Mascot, one discard spell and one multicolored spell. You have an 89% chance of seeing one of the 11 discard spells by turn 4, and a 68% chance of seeing an Eidolon.
- The deck has 14 white sources where Boros Aggro lists run about 16. That's on purpose: this deck needs red and white equally, unlike those mostly-white lists.
- The checker flagged Relic of Progenitus as rarely played. I kept it because it can exile a card from your own graveyard every turn for free, which gives Mascot a counter each time. It also hurts the Terror and graveyard decks.

The sideboard is aimed at the current top decks: Red Elemental Blast and Pyroblast for Terror and Faeries, Electrickery and Fire at Will for Madness and Elves, and Dust to Dust for Affinity and Wildfire.

--- After review ---
I took both fixes and resubmitted. The deck is legal at 60 cards with 19 lands (14 white sources, 14 red).

**What changed:**
1. **Boros Recruit (2) out, Wojek Halberdiers (2) in.** Halberdiers ({R}{W}, 3/2, gains first strike when it attacks with at least two other creatures) is a gold card, so casting it brings the Eidolons back just like Recruit did. It's a much better body. The cost: Recruit's hybrid {R/W} cost was only 1 mana, which made it easier to cast alongside an Eidolon in the same turn. I'll take the bigger creature over that.
2. **Relic of Progenitus (2) out, Skyknight Legionnaire (2) in.** Relic's tap can exile a card from your own yard to grow Mascot. But its other mode exiles all graveyards, which wipes your own Eidolons. It also never attacks. Legionnaire ({1}{R}{W}, 2/2 flying haste) is another gold cast that brings the Eidolons back, and it deals damage the turn it lands. That fits the turn-6 kill better. Graveyard hate still lives in the sideboard (Dust to Dust, Destroy Evil). Relic isn't there because the 15 slots were already full.

**Effect on the plan:** You now have 22 gold cards to bring the Eidolons back, up from 20. The curve is a little heavier: six cards at 3 mana instead of four, and 11 at 1 mana instead of 15.

**A note on the numbers:** The submit tool says you'll have drawn every card in the win line by turn 6 in only about 0.1% of games. That counts all eight named cards, and the deck doesn't need all of them. The real core is Mascot, a way to discard an Eidolon, and a gold spell to bring it back.

results.prompt: Brew me a Premodern deck built around Future Sight, Academy Rector and Veteran Explorer.
results.text:
I built a four-color (green, white, blue, red) "Rector Renewal" brew. All three cards you named make it in, but Future Sight is the backup engine, not the main kill.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **The Pattern Combo shell.** This was the only recent list running both Rector and Explorer. It's a Survival of the Fittest toolbox that grinds out value with Pattern of Rebirth and Recurring Nightmare. Future Sight would just be one more thing for Rector to fetch.
2. **The Enchantress/Replenish shell from the current results.** Rector is a weak fit there, and Explorer has nothing to do.
3. **What I chose: Pattern Combo's Survival + Goblin Bombardment + Rector base and mana, with an Enduring Renewal combo as the kill.** I picked this because it gives Rector a one-card kill to put directly onto the battlefield, and it lets Explorer's ramp pay for Future Sight's {2}{U}{U}{U}.

**The plan:**
- **Turn 1:** Veteran Explorer.
- **Turn 2:** Goblin Bombardment. Sacrifice Explorer to it: each player gets up to two basic lands, which come in untapped, so you can grab Islands for Future Sight or whatever colors you're missing.
- **Turn 3:** Cast Academy Rector with the extra mana.
- **Turn 4:** Sacrifice Rector to Bombardment and put Enduring Renewal onto the battlefield. Then cast Ornithopter or Shield Sphere (both cost 0), sacrifice it for 1 damage, and Renewal returns it to your hand. Repeat for infinite damage.

When you don't have the combo, Rector can fetch Future Sight instead, so you can play lands and spells off the top of your library. Enlightened Tutor finds Bombardment, Renewal, Future Sight or a 0-cost creature, and Survival of the Fittest finds Rector or the 0-drops.

**Things to know:**
- **Odds:** Drawing all six combo cards naturally by turn 4 happens in only about 0.1% of games. That number ignores tutors, and the deck runs 4 Enlightened Tutor, 4 Survival and 4 Rector to find the pieces. Bombardment itself shows up naturally by turn 4 only about 53% of the time, so expect a turn 4–6 kill most games, not a reliable turn 4.
- **Downsides:** Explorer ramps your opponent too, though they only get two basics. Stifle from Stiflenought, the biggest deck in the field, can counter the Rector or Explorer trigger.
- **The deck checker** flagged Enduring Renewal and Bombardment as rarely played. I kept them because they're the combo pieces, not filler.
- **Sideboard:** It targets the top of the field. Pyroblast is for Stiflenought and Standstill, Circle of Protection: Red, Spike Feeder and Ravenous Baloth are for Goblins and Sligh, and Seal of Cleansing is for Enchantress and Replenish.

results.prompt: Brew me a Premodern deck built around Utopia Tree, Rhystic Tutor and Bloodfire Colossus.
results.text:
I built a Jund (black-red-green) Survival Reanimator deck. It borrows the discard-and-reanimate shell from Premodern's Reanimator archetype (52 recent lists) and adds Survival of the Fittest from the BG Survival and Survival Madness decks.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Straight green ramp to 8 mana** (Utopia Tree, Birds of Paradise, Sneak Attack). Too slow against a field led by Stiflenought.
2. **Classic Reanimator** (Putrid Imp, Exhume, Dark Ritual). Fast, but Utopia Tree had no job in it.
3. **Survival plus reanimation (chosen).** This is the only direction where all three cards matter. Survival turns Utopia Tree into a way to find Bloodfire Colossus, and Dark Ritual lets you cast Rhystic Tutor on turn 1, before the opponent has 2 open mana to pay its tax.

**The plan:** Get Colossus into your graveyard on turns 1–2 using Putrid Imp, Survival of the Fittest or Buried Alive. Rhystic Tutor finds whichever piece is missing. Then put Colossus onto the battlefield with Exhume or Animate Dead for 2 mana. It beats down as a 6/6 (5/6 under Animate Dead). Its {R}-and-sacrifice ability wipes out boards from Goblins, Zoo or whatever the opponent got back with Exhume. Once the opponent is at 6 life or less, the same ability deals the final 6 damage. Animate Dead can bring Colossus back after it sacrifices itself.

**The cards you asked for:**
- **Utopia Tree:** makes any color (Colossus needs red off a mostly-Swamp mana base). It's also a creature to discard to Survival or sacrifice for Cabal Therapy's flashback.
- **Rhystic Tutor:** finds any card, unless any player pays 2. That makes it best on turn 1 off Dark Ritual and much worse later in the game.
- **Bloodfire Colossus:** I run 3 copies because you put it onto the battlefield from the graveyard instead of casting it, and three cards can find it.

**Odds and caveats:**
- **Opening hands:** by turn 3 on the play you have about a 92% chance to have seen a discard or tutor card and about 75% to have seen Exhume or Animate Dead.
- **Self-damage:** Colossus deals 6 damage to every player, you included. Plan your life total around it, especially since the painlands and City of Brass also hurt you. Don't fire it against burn decks like Sligh unless it wins on the spot.
- **Land count:** the checker flagged 16 lands. That's on purpose: real Reanimator lists run about 14, and this deck adds 8 mana creatures.
- **Win line stat:** the 0.7% figure counts the odds of drawing every card in the line. The line really needs any one card from each step, and tutors aren't simulated, so it isn't a real failure rate.

**Sideboard:**
- 4 Pyroblast against Stiflenought
- 2 Naturalize against Enchantress, Replenish and Oath
- 3 Tormod's Crypt against graveyard decks
- 2 Smother, 2 Snuff Out and 2 Engineered Plague against creature decks
